note: Nine atoms. band_adaptations from vault K-2/3-5/6-8 sections. Greet and Restorative marked pending — vault not yet band-sorted for those two.

strategies.label: Greet Students at the Door

band_adaptations.k2: Welcome song, morning meeting, or start-of-day ritual. (Band notes in progress.)
band_adaptations.35: By-name greeting at the door; bell work begins immediately inside. (Band notes in progress.)
band_adaptations.68: Hallway contact during transition; advisory check-in. (Band notes in progress.)

strategies.summary: Greeting students at the door is one example of an effective entry routine. The goal is not the greeting itself; the goal is creating a predictable transition from the hallway into learning.
solves: Unstructured transition time
Difficulty beginning class
Limited teacher-student connection
Lost instructional minutes
Lack of predictability
mechanism: Predictable routines reduce uncertainty — cognitive load drops
Students receive an immediate cue that learning has begun
Teachers gather quick information before instruction
Positive interactions strengthen relationships and belonging
Entry becomes intentional rather than accidental
strategies.evidence_note: Cook et al. (2018) found positive greetings raised academic engagement ~20 percentage points and reduced disruptive behavior ~9 points.

strategies.label: Restorative Interactions

band_adaptations.k2: More frequent, shorter contacts; built into morning circle or check-in ritual. (Band notes in progress.)
band_adaptations.35: Two minutes during independent work or transition; interest surveys as a starting point. (Band notes in progress.)
band_adaptations.68: Hallway or transition contact; text-based back-and-forth for students who prefer it over talk. (Band notes in progress.)

strategies.summary: Two minutes of non-academic conversation with one hard-to-reach student, held for ten consecutive school days. The goal is building a durable relationship with a student who is currently reachable only through the deed, not the person.
solves: A student who feels unseen or only-seen-when-in-trouble
Redirections that keep spending the bond instead of building it
A relationship that starts and stays in the negative
Escalating behavior with no relational channel to reach through
mechanism: Ten consecutive days signals reliability — the student learns the adult keeps coming back
Non-academic content means the interaction is not about compliance
Repeated positive contact builds relationship before the next hard moment
strategies.evidence_note: Wlodkowski's 85% improvement figure is practitioner-reported and illustrative, not a measured finding.

strategies.label: Co-Created Norms

band_adaptations.k2: Read-aloud to values — picture book about friendship or fairness, then 'how do we want our room to feel?' Answers become an illustrated anchor chart, signed.
band_adaptations.35: Students draft in small groups, cluster ideas into shared expectations, and sign the agreement. Posted and revisited regularly.
band_adaptations.68: Discuss why norms matter first — what a good room feels like, what erodes it — then co-write and commit.

strategies.summary: A class agreement authored with students. The goal is not the list on the wall; the goal is authorship. Students who help write the norms hold them, because they own them.
solves: Expectations that students follow but do not believe
Rules that feel imposed rather than shared
Weak buy-in when a teacher hands down a posted list
mechanism: Authorship creates ownership — students hold norms they helped write
Autonomy of authorship feeds motivation (SoL Q4)
Shared expectations reduce extraneous cognitive load
strategies.evidence_note: Grounded in autonomy mechanisms (SoL Q4) and belonging-through-co-authorship (Klevan 2021).

strategies.label: Teach the Transition

band_adaptations.k2: Attach the sequence to a song, chant, or counted signal; pair it with a picture schedule.
band_adaptations.35: Students manage their own materials inside the sequence; introduce a visible timer.
band_adaptations.68: Fewer steps, stated once, then handed over — students set the norm for what a clean move looks like.

strategies.summary: A transition is taught and rehearsed the way content is taught — modeled, practiced, and named — rather than announced once and enforced afterward.
solves: The seam between activities is where most instructional time leaks
Students stall at the boundary not because they're refusing but because they don't know the next action
The teacher ends up narrating every move, which makes the class dependent on the narration
mechanism: A rehearsed sequence runs from memory rather than being assembled on the spot — working memory is freed
Each rehearsal is a low-stakes retrieval of the sequence (SoL Q1)
Teaching the move in advance means the teacher shapes the moment rather than correcting after it
strategies.evidence_note: Kounin (1970) established momentum and smoothness — well-managed classrooms anticipate friction at activity boundaries rather than reacting to it.

strategies.label: The Repair Conversation

band_adaptations.k2: Two questions only: what happened, what would help. Concrete restitution the child can physically do.
band_adaptations.35: All four questions, teacher-facilitated. Introduce the apology-of-action.
band_adaptations.68: Students can facilitate for peers. Privacy matters most at this age.

strategies.summary: A short, structured conversation after harm, built on four questions that surface what happened and what would make it right. The goal is not an apology; the goal is that the student stays inside the community that has to keep working after the incident.
solves: Something happened and the room can't just proceed as if it didn't
The available responses feel like a choice between letting it go and removing someone
A forced apology gets produced and nothing about tomorrow is different
mechanism: Who does the accounting: in a repair conversation the student constructs the account
Naming who was affected makes the harm concrete and external
The student stays inside relationships and belonging, which is the channel any future correction has to travel through
strategies.evidence_note: Exclusionary discipline is associated with increased future misbehavior and dropout risk (Klevan 2021).

strategies.label: Design the Room Around the Work
aliases: Design the Room Around the Work

band_adaptations.k2: Clearly defined areas, wide clear paths, materials at child height, deliberately low visual clutter.
band_adaptations.35: Flexible groupings inside a set structure; student materials jobs; a designated gather space.
band_adaptations.68: Configurations that flex from rows to groups to circle with minimal disruption — the reconfiguration itself is a rehearsed move.

strategies.summary: Arrange furniture, materials, and traffic paths around what students actually do in the room. The goal is not a tidy room; the goal is that the easiest physical action is also the one the lesson needs.
solves: Minutes disappear into retrieving, distributing, and returning materials
The same two spots generate friction every day and it reads as behavior
Moving between formats takes long enough that teachers stop doing it
mechanism: Materials placed where the work happens remove a whole class of interruptions before they occur
A room that can become a circle makes community and repair structurally possible
Equitable sightlines and access say every student is included by default
strategies.evidence_note: The strong claims are about mechanisms — attention capture, load, access — rather than any particular furniture arrangement.

strategies.label: Post What You'd Otherwise Repeat

band_adaptations.k2: Picture schedules and icon cues at child eye level — the image is the instruction, not a caption.
band_adaptations.35: Anchor charts co-built with students during the lesson; posted step sequences for multi-step tasks.
band_adaptations.68: Objectives and agenda posted on entry; reference charts students consult independently without being told to.

strategies.summary: Make visible the information students would otherwise have to hold in their heads or ask you for. The goal is not a decorated wall; the goal is that the room carries the information so working memory doesn't have to.
solves: The same question gets asked five times an hour about something already said
A multi-step task stalls halfway because the middle steps have fallen out of memory
Transitions require the teacher to narrate what's next, every time
mechanism: A posted sequence is external memory — steps are read rather than recalled (SoL Q1)
Dual-channel representation (visual + verbal) supports learning better than either alone
Predictability is a safety condition — a student who can see what's coming isn't managing threat
strategies.evidence_note: The honest claim is narrow: a specific visual, referencing taught content, available at the moment of need, reduces load.

strategies.label: Third Point Feedback

band_adaptations.k2: The third point is concrete — the actual paper, a picture of 'finished,' a two-item checklist. Acknowledge the process pointed at the work.
band_adaptations.35: Peer feedback with stems aimed at criteria rather than each other — 'here's what you did, why it matters, you might try.'
band_adaptations.68: Student self-assesses against criteria first; the conference compares two readings. Feedback delivered privately — peers hearing it re-introduces the ego threat.

strategies.summary: Aim the feedback at a shared external reference — a rubric, a model, the criteria, the work itself — rather than at the student. The goal is not softer criticism; the goal is that the student can evaluate the work without defending themselves.
solves: Accurate feedback gets rejected — the student hears a judgment about them and stops listening
A conference turns into reassurance because the honest version would feel like an attack
Revision doesn't happen because accepting the feedback would mean accepting the verdict that came with it
mechanism: Ego-threat feedback is rejected regardless of accuracy (SoL Q2)
Feedback gives the student goal, current position, and next step (Hattie & Timperley, 2007)
Same structure as naming the deed, not the doer
strategies.evidence_note: 'Third point' is a practitioner framing. What's evidence-backed is the mechanism: ego threat blocks uptake, and task-focused feedback outperforms person-focused feedback.

strategies.label: Everybody Answers

band_adaptations.k2: Whole-body and signal responses — thumbs, cards, hand on head — before anyone speaks. Response cards. Partner talk in short bursts.
band_adaptations.35: Sticky-note responses, think-then-all-hands, students teaching a strategy to a partner. Introduce the norm that everyone answers something before anyone answers aloud.
band_adaptations.68: Written commitment before discussion; structured protocols where each person has a turn. At this age, cold-calling without the pre-answer step costs face and the cost is remembered.

strategies.summary: Structure the question so every student produces an answer — on paper, to a partner, with a signal — before anyone shares aloud. The goal is not more hands up; the goal is that every student has actually retrieved something, because retrieval is where the learning happens.
solves: The same four students answer everything, and the room reads as engaged because they are
A student who's lost has no low-risk way to try, so they wait it out
The lesson runs on the student most willing to talk
mechanism: Every student retrieves — the learning is in the retrieval, not in the answer given aloud (SoL Q1/Q2)
Low-risk formats lower the stakes of being wrong, which is a prerequisite for trying
A structure where every voice is expected is a belonging condition
strategies.evidence_note: Grounded in retrieval practice (SoL Q1/Q2) and competence-before-buy-in. NOT grounded in response rate or OTR literature — a response-rate framing optimizes for frequency and produces fast shallow questioning.
